## Compute $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Z})$

**Claim:** $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Z}) = \{0\}$, the trivial group.

**Proof.**

Let $f \colon \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a homomorphism of additive groups. We show $f$ is identically zero.

Fix an arbitrary $q \in \mathbb{Q}$. For every positive integer $n \geq 1$, since $\mathbb{Q}$ is divisible, the element $q/n \in \mathbb{Q}$ satisfies
$$n \cdot \frac{q}{n} = q.$$
Applying the homomorphism $f$ and using $\mathbb{Z}$-linearity (i.e., $f(n \cdot x) = n \cdot f(x)$ for $x \in \mathbb{Q}$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$):
$$f(q) = f\!\left(n \cdot \frac{q}{n}\right) = n \cdot f\!\left(\frac{q}{n}\right).$$
Since $f(q/n) \in \mathbb{Z}$, this shows that $f(q)$ is an integer divisible by $n$.

This holds for **every** positive integer $n$. The only integer divisible by every positive integer $n$ is $0$ (since a nonzero integer $m$ has $|m| \geq 1$, and taking $n = |m| + 1 > |m|$ makes divisibility impossible unless $m = 0$). Therefore
$$f(q) = 0.$$

Since $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ was arbitrary, $f \equiv 0$. The only homomorphism $\mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Z}$ is the zero map, so
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Z}) = \{0\}.$$

**Remark (structural viewpoint).** This is a special case of the general fact that $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(D, A) = 0$ whenever $D$ is a divisible group and $A$ is a **reduced** group (one with no nonzero divisible subgroups). The additive group $\mathbb{Q}$ is divisible, and $\mathbb{Z}$ is reduced (it has no nonzero divisible subgroup, since no nonzero integer is divisible by all $n$). The argument above is exactly the instantiation of this general principle.

### PROOF COMPLETE
